title: Corpus-Based Problem Selection for EHR Note Summarization
research_question: Can corpus-derived lexical, frequency, persistence, and temporal features identify which clinical problems from longitudinal notes should be retained in a concise patient summary?
methodology: The authors formulate problem selection as binary classification after using MedLEE and UMLS/SNOMED resources to identify candidate clinical problems in notes. They train primarily on a renal outpatient corpus of 1,618 patients averaging 14.3 notes per patient, using the final past-medical-history section as a scalable surrogate for summary-relevant problems, and separately evaluate against nephrologist-authored summaries for four patients. Naive Bayes and C4.5 classifiers, multiple feature-selection schemes, section restrictions, concept grouping, and negation filtering are evaluated with precision, recall, F-measure, F2, error rates, and confidence intervals.

key_findings.finding: The best reported relevance-classification accuracy reached 82%, with an F-measure of 0.62.
Restricting candidate evidence to particular note sections significantly reduced F-measure rather than improving selection.
A simple filter for problems that were predominantly or finally negated improved both precision and recall in the reported experiments.
When precision and recall were weighted equally, best-first feature selection helped remove extraneous problems from the proposed summary.
When recall was weighted more heavily through F2, omitting feature selection produced better results, showing that the preferred selector depends on the cost assigned to omissions.
Features describing note-level usage patterns were more useful than temporal-duration features in this corpus, although the authors caution that the renal corpus covered a relatively short period.
Fine-grained and inconsistent concept coding complicated matching between source notes, classifier concepts, and expert-summary references.

limitations: The large training corpus uses the final past-medical-history section as a surrogate gold standard rather than a purpose-written longitudinal summary.
Direct expert-summary evaluation involved only four renal patients.
The principal corpus comes from one outpatient renal service at NewYork-Presbyterian, limiting demonstrated specialty and institutional generalizability.
The renal corpus covers a relatively short period, which may disadvantage temporal-duration features.
UMLS/SNOMED coding granularity can split semantically similar problems into different identifiers and confound both classification and evaluation.
Experiments for grouping related concepts were inconclusive.
Problems present in expert summaries but absent from source notes were excluded from evaluation, narrowing the assessed task.
The study selects problems for a summary rather than generating and evaluating a complete coherent longitudinal narrative.
raw_claims: The task is formulated as deciding, for every clinical problem mentioned in a patient's notes, whether it belongs in a summary.
MedLEE is used to identify clinical concepts and information about negation.
The main renal corpus contains 1,618 patients with an average of 14.3 notes per patient.
The final past-medical-history section is used as a scalable surrogate for summary relevance during training.
Nephrologists independently authored summaries for four patients for expert-based evaluation.
Precision, recall, F-measure, F2, and error-based measures are used to assess problem selection.
Restricting extraction to individual note sections reduced F-measure.
Filtering problems that were generally negated improved precision and recall.
Best-first feature selection was useful when precision and recall were valued equally.
When missing a relevant problem was given greater cost, using all features produced better F2 results.
Note-frequency and usage features were stronger than temporal-duration features in the studied corpus.
Concept-coding granularity created matching and evaluation errors.
The best reported relevance classification accuracy was 82%.
